papers.title: Designing stimuli for non-invasive, cell-type-specific manipulation of retinal ganglion cell activity
papers.abstract: The retina encodes visual information through parallel pathways formed by distinct retinal ganglion (RGC) types. Current understanding of how each cell type contributes to downstream visual processing and perception is limited by a lack of tools for selectively manipulating the activities of individual RGC types. Here, we introduce a computational framework called STORM (SpatioTemporal Orthogonal Response Modulation) that creates visual stimuli that aim to selectively modulate the activities of specific RGC types while minimally affecting the activities of nearby RGCs of non-targeted types. To illustrate the approach, demonstrate its flexibility, and identify conditions under which each simulated RGC type could be selectively manipulated, we first applied this framework to simplified models of RGC function, such as Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) and LN-LN cascade models. We also deployed this approach on more complex (and more accurate) models of RGC responses, based on convolutional neural networks. We demonstrate that differences in spatial receptive fields, temporal dynamics, response polarities, and nonlinearities can provide sufficient degrees of freedom for designing stimuli that selectively manipulate individual RGC types. We also generalize this approach to conditions where the receptive field locations are unknown for in vivo and clinical applications.

papers.title: Targeting microglial P2Y12-receptor signalling attenuates neurodegeneration in experimental Parkinsons disease
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as a determinant of dopaminergic neuron vulnerability in Parkinson's disease, yet the receptor-level mechanisms linking microglia to disease progression remain incompletely defined. We investigated whether microglial P2Y12 receptor (P2Y12R) signalling drives neurodegeneration in experimental Parkinsonism and assessed its pharmacological tractability. Tamoxifen-inducible microglia-specific P2ry12 deletion was examined in acute and subchronic MPTP models, with receptor deletion induced before or during disease progression. Neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, neurochemistry, and motor function were evaluated, and novel P2Y12R antagonists identified by structure-based virtual screening were characterized in vitro and following central administration in vivo. Inducible microglia-specific P2Y12R deletion reduced nigrostriatal dopaminergic neuron loss, preserved dopamine synthesis, attenuated acute and sustained neuroinflammatory responses, and improved parkinsonian motor deficits without affecting survival. Importantly, delayed receptor deletion during ongoing neurodegeneration remained protective, indicating that P2Y12R contributes to disease progression. Two novel antagonists exhibited functional P2Y12R inhibition in vitro, and central administration of the most promising candidate recapitulated the neuroprotective phenotype observed following genetic receptor deletion. These findings identify microglial P2Y12R as a therapeutically relevant regulator of neuroinflammation and dopaminergic vulnerability and provide complementary genetic and pharmacological proof-of-concept for targeting central P2Y12R in Parkinsonism.

papers.title: Reactivation of neural signatures of food during REM-like sleep in the high-level visual cortex of monkeys
papers.abstract: Vision and its neural basis have always been studied in animals that are artificially restrained to obtain stable neural recordings. This approach, while insightful, precludes understanding behaviors like sleep that take place only in natural settings. What happens to neurons in the high-level visual cortex during sleep? Do neural responses to objects seen while awake get reactivated during sleep, just like navigation replay in the hippocampus? To investigate these issues, we performed wireless neural recordings from the high-level visual (IT) and motor regions (PMv, PFC) in two monkeys while they performed a fixation task in which they viewed food images and subsequently slept in their natural setting. Decoders trained on neural activity were able to predict the sleep/wake state as well as transitions between states well in advance. Importantly, decoders trained on neural responses to food images (but not faces/objects) showed higher food probability during REM-like sleep compared to NREM or awake states, suggesting that the monkeys dreamt about food. Thus, neural signatures of food seen while awake are reactivated during sleep.

papers.title: Palmitoylation of p75 neurotrophin receptor is required for retrograde regressive signaling
papers.abstract: Target-derived neurotrophins regulate neuronal survival and pruning via retrograde signaling. Unlike Trk receptors, which are transported as transmembrane proteins, the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) undergoes regulated intramembrane proteolysis to release a soluble intracellular domain (ICD) that must somehow associate with axonal endosomes for retrograde transport. Here, we identify palmitoylation of a conserved juxta membrane cysteine (C281) as a critical requirement for this process. In sympathetic neurons, we demonstrate that p75NTR palmitoylation is dispensable for surface trafficking and proteolytic cleavage but is strictly required for ligand-induced internalization and the biogenesis of p75ICD-positive signaling endosomes. Consequently, blocking palmitoylation, either pharmacologically or via a palmitoylation-deficient C281A mutation, prevents the accumulation of p75ICD in axonal endosomes and blocks axon-initiated apoptosis. In vivo, C281A knock-in mice exhibit reduced developmental apoptosis of sympathetic neurons, similar to p75NTR deletion. These findings define palmitoylation as an essential checkpoint that couples p75NTR cleavage to endosomal segregation, thereby enabling the long-distance transmission of regressive signals.

papers.title: Objective markers of altered neural gain dissociate tinnitus and self-reported listening problems in individuals with exceptional hearing thresholds
papers.abstract: Many individuals experience problems that are undetected by standard hearing tests, such as persistent tinnitus and difficulties understanding speech in background noise. Here, we report evidence of altered neural gain in young adults with self-reported listening problems despite exceptional hearing thresholds. Individuals reporting persistent tinnitus (the daily percept of sound in the absence of an external source) exhibited elevated thresholds of the middle ear muscle reflex, suggestive of altered gain in brainstem reflexive circuits, and reduced cortical responses to auditory spatial cues conveyed in the temporal fine structure of low-frequency sounds. Moreover, in both groups, greater self-reported speech-in-noise difficulties were associated with higher magnitude cortical responses, particularly at the highest stimulus intensity, consistent with elevated neural gain. Using a conceptual model, we demonstrate how damage to high-threshold auditory nerve fibres innervating cochlear nuclei can account for reduced activity of binaural neurons sensitive to the temporal fine structure of low-frequency sounds, generating a compensatory increase in neural gain in higher brain centres that impacts listening in complex environments.

papers.title: Cell-intrinsic regulation of presynaptic release site patterning
papers.abstract: Functional neuronal connectivity depends not only on synaptic partner choice but also on the number, strength, and spatial distribution of release sites between partners. How these features are regulated remains poorly understood. Here, using the C. elegans DA9 motor neuron, we identify the immunoglobulin superfamily cell adhesion molecules SYG-1 and SYG-2 as cell-autonomous regulators of presynaptic release-site patterning. SYG-2 regulates presynapse number, size, and spacing, whereas SYG-1 primarily regulates spacing. Endogenous localization and cell-specific knockout analyses reveal that SYG-2 recruits SYG-1 to the presynaptic domain through previously unrecognized cis interactions. Endogenous structure-function studies further demonstrate that the SYG-2 intracellular domain is required for presynaptic organization and can promote presynapse formation independently of its extracellular domain. Genetic and targeted actin-disruption experiments implicate the adaptor protein NCK-1 and local actin remodeling in SYG-2 intracellular signaling. Together, these findings reveal how cell adhesion molecules can act cell-intrinsically to pattern presynaptic release sites after synaptic partners have been established.

papers.title: Disease stage-sensitive MFSD2A-caveolae axis insigates hippocampal blood-brain barrier disruption in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) malfunction contributes to pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms that confer hippocampal endotheliocytes vulnerability remain unclear. Here we identify loss of endothelial major facilitator superfamily domain-containing protein 2A (MFSD2A), a suppressor of caveolae-mediated transcytosis, as an early and hippocampus-specific feature of AD-associated vascular impairment. In post-mortem human AD brains, reduction in hippocampal MFSD2A was accompanied with increased levels of caveolin-1 and perivascular albumin extravasation. Analysis of human single-nucleus transcriptomic data further demonstrated that vascular expression of MFSD2A declined during transition from mild cognitive impairment to established AD. In APP/PS1 mice, MFSD2A loss occurred early in hippocampal microvessels and coincided with disproportionately high hippocampal BBB leakage and reductions in GLUT1 and claudin-5, despite broader amyloid deposition throughout other brain regions. Restoration of endothelial MFSD2A using an AAV-BR1-based vascular vector during early stage of amyloid pathology, reduced albumin extravasation and preserved GLUT1 and claudin-5. Early intervention also reduced amyloid plaque burden and plaque-associated neuritic dystrophy, whereas this treatment during established amyloid pathology, although modifying selected endothelial markers, failed to reverse BBB leakage, amyloid pathology, or cognitive impairment. Sustained MFSD2A restoration from the early disease stage provided the greatest protection, preserving hippocampal BBB integrity, reducing amyloid and neuritic pathology, improving long-term potentiation and ameliorating spatial learning and memory deficits. These findings define endothelial MFSD2A loss as a disease stage-sensitive mechanism of hippocampal BBB vulnerability and highlight the MFSD2A-caveolae axis as a therapeutic target for early-stage AD.

papers.title: RAPTOR-targeted Antisense Oligonucleotides Restrict Pathological mTORC1 Activity in GATOR1-dependent Disease
papers.abstract: Loss-of-function mutations in the GATOR1 complex (NPRL2, NPRL3, and DEPDC5) are among the most common genetic causes of epilepsy. These mutations impair amino acid-dependent regulation of mTORC1 and cause hyperactive signaling, neuronal hyperexcitability, astrocytic metabolic remodeling, seizures, and early mortality. Here, we report the development of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting RAPTOR, an mTORC1 scaffolding subunit, to correct pathological mTORC1 hyperactivity caused by defective upstream regulation. RAPTOR-targeted ASO treatment reduced RAPTOR expression in mouse and human systems and dampened mTORC1 signaling in GATOR1-deficient models. ASO-mediated RAPTOR reduction rescued neuronal hyperexcitability, corrected astrocytic mitochondrial dysfunction, and suppressed spontaneous seizures in vivo. A single treatment significantly extended longevity across neuronal and astrocytic models of GATOR1 deficiency. Collectively, these findings establish RAPTOR-targeted ASOs as a mechanism-based therapeutic approach that durably corrects cellular and circuit-level consequences of GATOR1 deficiency. By tuning RAPTOR abundance, this strategy provides a therapeutic framework for mTORC1-driven epilepsies and related diseases.

papers.title: MICROSTRUCTURAL ORGANIZATION OF CORTICO-SUBCORTICAL FUNCTIONAL CONVERGENCE
papers.abstract: The human subcortex integrates information from distributed cortical regions through functionally organized cortico-subcortical systems. Using the publicly available MICA-MICs multimodal MRI dataset of 50 healthy adults, we characterized the microstructural organization of functionally converging cortical regions. First, using resting-state fMRI., we identified cortical regions converging on subcortical targets, including thalamic, basal ganglia, and subcortical limbic structures. Then, using depth-resolved quantitative T1 profiles, we constructed a convergence-restricted microstructural profile covariance matrix, followed by diffusion-map embedding. The first microstructural gradient predominantly differentiated primary and association cortex, whereas the second gradient showed target-related differentiation beyond differences in primary versus association cortex. Cytoarchitectural analysis further revealed target-related differences in cortical composition. Together, these findings reveal complementary dimensions of cortico-subcortical functional organization, spanning broad cortical hierarchy, target-related microstructural differentiation, and cytoarchitectural composition.

papers.title: Preconceptional social isolation alters inflammatory and transcriptional signalling across the placenta-fetal brain axis
papers.abstract: Maternal depression and psychosocial adversity during pregnancy are associated with altered offspring neurodevelopment, yet the molecular processes linking maternal state to the developing fetus remain incompletely understood. The placenta is positioned to sense and respond to maternal physiological signals, but how placental molecular responses relate to those in the developing brain is unclear. Here, we used a mouse model of prolonged social isolation initiated before conception and maintained throughout pregnancy to investigate inflammatory and transcriptional alterations across matched placenta and fetal-brain samples at gestational day 18. Maternal social isolation altered cytokine profiles in both tissues and induced extensive transcriptional changes in the placenta, with a more restricted response in the fetal brain. Functional analyses identified alterations in placental immune, metabolic and transport-related programmes and fetal-brain immune, neuronal and proliferative processes. Although sex-stratified analyses revealed different transcriptional profiles in male and female tissues, formal maternal housing x fetal-sex interaction testing did not identify significant gene-level interaction effects. Cross-tissue co-expression analysis initially identified extensive covariation between social-isolation-responsive placental and fetal-brain modules; however, most associations were attenuated after accounting for their shared relationship with maternal housing. An exposure-independent network analysis nevertheless identified an inverse pregnancy-level association between a placental module enriched for immune and interferon-related signalling and a fetal-brain module enriched for cell-cycle and proliferative processes. Together, these findings show that prolonged maternal social adversity is associated with coordinated but tissue-distinct molecular alterations across the placenta-fetal brain axis and demonstrate the importance of distinguishing parallel responses to a common maternal environment from direct cross-tissue molecular coupling.

papers.title: Expert and Novice Visuomotor Strategies in a Sequential Football Task Reflect Distinct Generative Models
papers.abstract: In visuomotor sequential tasks, chaining actions smoothly requires tight coordination between sensory and motor systems to deal with competing demands, such as reducing uncertainty about future opportunities for action while controlling ongoing ones. In a football-based decision-making task, experts and novices used different strategies to overcome these competing demands, demonstrating a proactive and a sequential visuomotor strategy, respectively. We propose a computational explanation of expertise-related difference in policy selection, grounded in the active inference framework. We simulated the selection of sequence of actions using a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) model, and we manipulated three parameters: the reward structure, the prior beliefs about state transition, and the sensory precision. Simulations showed that selection of the proactive strategy relied on strong prior beliefs, high sensory precision and high valuation of fast passing. Conversely, the sequential policy was selected when rapid performance was not highly valued, or under noisy prior beliefs, or lower level of sensory precision. Decreasing sensory precision and adding noise in prior beliefs also decreased decision accuracy. These results suggest that policy selection leading to novice or expert visuomotor strategy reflects differences in the underlying generative model, particularly in how agents value different aspects of the task.

papers.title: Glia-enriched human brain organoids for studying developmental alterations in leukodystrophies
papers.abstract: Leukodystrophies (LKD) comprise mostly inherited white matter disorders whose developmental origins and underlying pathomechanisms remain poorly understood. Progress has been limited by restricted access to human primary tissue and by the inability of animal models to fully recapitulate human neurodevelopment. Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural organoids provide an alternative approach, but most culture systems do not capture later, glia-rich developmental stages relevant to these diseases. Recent studies have shown that appropriate patterning cues and long in vitro differentiation can generate neuroglial spheroids comprising multiple neuronal and macroglial populations, including mature oligodendrocytes. Here, we adapt the human oligodendrocyte (hOLS) spheroid platform to establish 3D models of globoid cell leukodystrophy (GLD), 4H leukodystrophy (4H), and Canavan disease (CD). Here we adapt this organoid platform to establish 3D models of globoid cell leukodystrophy (GLD), 4H leukodystrophy (4H), and Canavan disease (CD). Across 150 days of differentiation, hOLS from different genetic backgrounds displayed largely comparable growth kinetics and developmental trajectories, comprising multiple neuroglial cell types with predominantly ventral forebrain and midbrain identities. Comparison of LKD and control hOLS revealed both shared and disease-specific alterations, with prominent transcriptional changes in lysosomal, metabolic, and stress-response pathways. Lineage-resolved pathway analysis further identified signatures across individual LKDs, including mitochondrial and translational stress in GLD glial lineages, disruption of RNA metabolic and cell-cycle pathways in 4H, and prominent astrocyte-centered metabolic dysregulation in CD. Our results establish hOLS as a human 3D in vitro platform for studying the impact of LKD-associated genetic variants on early neural development and for dissecting lineage-specific disease vulnerability.

papers.title: Computer mouse weight is associated with one-week motor skill improvement in a large naturalistic video game cohort
papers.abstract: Computer mouse weight has been proposed to influence human motor performance, but existing evidence comes largely from small, short-duration controlled studies, leaving its relationship to performance during naturalistic gameplay unresolved. We analyzed one-week skill improvement in Aimlabs, a popular first-person shooter aim-training and assessment platform, among 9,067 players whose telemetry recorded a mouse-model change (switchers) during self-directed game use, using a 21-day baseline and 7-day follow-up; 4,991 players with a single mouse model (non-switchers) observed over matched pseudo-anchor intervals provided a secondary contextual comparison. Post-switch mouse weight was represented by eight bands spanning 35-124 g. The primary multivariable generalized additive regression model accounted for baseline skill, pre- and post-switch practice intensity, and pre- and post-switch mouse sensitivity, and allowed the association between weight band and improvement to vary with baseline skill, post-switch practice, and post-switch sensitivity. For each weight band, predicted mean one-week improvement was standardized to the observed distribution of these covariates among switchers and reported in percentile-rank points. Statistical significance was evaluated using 1,000 permutations in which observed mouse weights were randomly reassigned among switchers without replacement and the model was refitted to generate empirical null distributions for the weight-related test statistics. Predicted improvement differed significantly across the eight weight bands (p = 0.001). Pairwise comparisons identified significant differences between bands (p < 0.05), but no single band was associated with significantly greater predicted improvement than all seven others. In this large naturalistic cohort, predicted improvement was highest for players with 35-44 g mice, followed by 45-54 and 55-64 g, and several pairwise comparisons showed significantly greater improvement in lighter than in heavier weight bands. Across the examined baseline-skill profiles, the lowest predicted improvements occurred in either the 85-99 or 115-124 g band. Predicted improvement differed across weight bands at the 25th-percentile and median baseline-skill values (p = 0.002 and p = 0.003) but not at the 75th percentile (p = 0.153). However, the weight-band x baseline-skill interaction was not significant (p = 0.181), indicating that the analysis did not establish that weight-related differences varied by skill level.

papers.title: Dual ecological-cultural pathways of sociocultural environment and resting state functional connectivity among Hispanic adolescents in the ABCD Study
papers.abstract: Hispanic Americans face persistent health disparities rooted in complex sociocultural and bioecodevelopmental dynamics. Identifying early neurodevelopmental trajectories that confer risk or resilience during adolescence is critical for developing targeted health equity interventions. Grounded in the NIMHD Research Framework and bioecodevelopmental theory, data from 12- to 14-year-old Hispanic adolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study were analyzed (n=236). Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) was used to evaluate multivariate associations between sociocultural measures, spanning individual, family, and community levels, and resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) networks. Post hoc linear mixed-effects models examined how derived sociocultural-rsFC patterns predicted measures of physical and mental health, linking bioecodevelopmental patterns to adolescent well-being. PLSC revealed dual community- and family-level neural pathways of biological embedding, diverging from traditional nested bioecodevelopmental assumptions. The community pathway linked child opportunity and neighborhood disadvantage to connectivity across Cingulo-Opercular, Default, Dorsal Attention, Visual Networks. This community-rsFC profile was associated with lower respiratory functioning, reflecting an allostatic load marker of environmental stress. The family pathway linked caregiver ethnic identity and heritage acculturation to Default, Ventral Attention, Sensorimotor-Mouth, and Visual Networks connectivity, suggesting that the family system shapes neural systems underlying social attunement and identity formation. Structural community factors and familial culture impose distinct neurobiological demands on the adolescent connectome among Hispanic youth. Findings highlight respiratory health as a biological marker of environmental adversity and underscore the necessity of structural and culturally sustaining interventions to promote health equity among Hispanic youth.

papers.title: Neural latent representation of implicit perceptual decision confidence signatures from brain-wide intracranial EEG
papers.abstract: Human perceptual decision confidence has been associated with brain-wide signalling, albeit with inconsistencies across studies. It remains unclear whether more robust neural latent representations exist, particularly for implicit confidence. We address this by applying complementary machine learning approaches to comprehensive, brain-wide intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) data acquired without explicit confidence reports. Using explainable feature selection methods, we elucidated key spatiotemporal iEEG components, especially in the frontal cortex, that readily distinguished confidence characteristics related to decision correctness, difficulty, and speed, and that were transferable across motor modalities. Despite inconsistencies in the features identified across methods and conditions, dimensionality reductions revealed robust low-dimensional neural latent representations. Furthermore, their neural trajectories within a shared subspace enhanced the distinguishability of confidence characteristics. Overall, our results uncover low-dimensional spatial and temporal neural latent representations underlying human implicit perceptual decision confidence that are robust to analytical methods and decision conditions.

papers.title: The effects of temporal smoothing and interpolation on EEG microstate parameters, syntax, and our view of resting-state brain dynamics
papers.abstract: Microstate analysis studies dynamic brain activity through a discrete representation of electroencephalographic (EEG) signals and their topography. While the body of literature describing findings in diverse experimental and clinical settings is growing rapidly, the effects of several core components of the microstate algorithm are still insufficiently understood. This study systematically investigates how two common temporal smoothing algorithms, parametric smoothing and GFP peak interpolation, influence a wide range of microstate sequence parameters, and how they shape the integrated picture of brain dynamics inferred from these metrics. We study eyes-closed resting-state EEG recordings from N=201 healthy subjects from a public EEG database. For the elementary temporal metrics, we find that widening smoothing windows markedly increase microstate duration, reduce occurrence rates, but leave coverage mostly unaffected. In terms of simple syntax properties, smoothing windows above 30 ms yield an inconsistent picture with a memoryless, first-order Markov structure at short time scales, but a positive Hurst phenomenon suggestive of long-range correlations at long time scales. Evidence of asymmetry and non-equilibrium dynamics are suppressed by smoothing. At intermediate time scales, microstate periodicity was only observed up to a window size of 28 ms. Smoothing had a strong impact on the complexity metrics entropy rate and excess entropy, decreasing the former and increasing the latter. For most metrics, the effects of GFP peak interpolation were comparable to those of smoothing windows in the range between 28 ms and 44 ms. In conclusion, elementary and higher-order microstate parameters must be interpreted in the context of preprocessing, as many parameters change continuously with smoothing intensity. This limits the comparability of microstate parameters obtained with different preprocessing settings. Strong smoothing with a window size above 30 ms or GFP peak interpolation yields a fundamentally different picture of resting state brain dynamics, i.e. that of a memoryless, aperiodic, time-reversible first-order Markov chain. Since insights from other neurophysiological modalities suggest that time series memory and time-irreversibility are markers of normal brain activity, our recommendation is to avoid intense smoothing to minimize alterations of the initial sequences.

papers.title: Age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across time of day, chronotype, and testing format
papers.abstract: Older adults typically exhibit reduced episodic memory precision, while maintaining relatively preserved retrieval success. However, little is known about whether these age-related differences are influenced by internal biological factors (e.g., chronotype) or external testing conditions (e.g., experiment format, time of day). To address this question, younger and older adults completed an object-location memory task online, either in the morning or evening, and either with or without video-based supervision. Memory performance was assessed using mean absolute error and Bayesian hierarchical mixture modelling, which dissociated memory precision ({kappa}) from the probability of memory-based responding ({theta}). Immediate memory performance was high across age groups, irrespective of time of day. Greater encoding error predicted greater retrieval error, and participants tested in the video condition exhibited lower recall error and higher recognition performance than those tested without supervision. Consistent with prior studies, older adults exhibited reduced memory precision relative to younger adults, whereas retrieval success remained largely intact. However, Bayesian Hierarchical Modelling provided no evidence that time of day, experiment format, or their interactions with age influenced either memory precision or retrieval probability. Older adults reported stronger morning preferences than younger adults, and participants generally selected testing times that aligned with their chronotype. Nevertheless, alignment between chronotype and testing time did not modulate memory performance. The results indicate that age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across variations in testing context, including time of day, experiment format, and individual differences in chronotype. More broadly, the results support the feasibility of remote and unsupervised testing for memory precision research and suggest that chronotype and testing time are unlikely to be major sources of variability in immediate object-location memory performance.

papers.title: Neuropeptide NLP-40 and Cognate G- Protein Coupled Receptor AEX-2 Regulate Behavioral Responses During Anoxia in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Background: Insufficient oxygen (hypoxia) or complete lack of oxygen (anoxia) causes cellular dysfunction and death in terrestrial animals. As a result, animals have developed homeostatic strategies, including changes in movement strategies to escape and survive stressful environments. Caenorhabditis elegans respond to changes in oxygen by increasing the frequency of reversals (backward movement) and increasing locomotor speed; these behaviors enable them to escape unfavorable environments and move to more suitable ones. The molecular and neural mechanisms underlying behavioral responses to low-oxygen environments are incomplete. Neuropeptides regulate C. elegans behaviors by modifying neural circuit function in response to hypoxia. Loss of function in C. elegans neuropeptide nlp-40 and its receptor aex-2 increased survival to anoxia [1]. However, the cells in which NLP-40 and AEX-2 function for anoxia, as well as the mechanisms underlying responses to anoxia, remain elusive. We hypothesized that NLP-40 and AEX-2 regulate anoxia by altering escape behaviors. Results: We found that neuropeptide NLP-40 functions in cholinergic neurons and AEX-2 functions in cholinergic or GLR-1 interneurons or motor neurons to regulate susceptibility to anoxia. We found that loss of either nlp-40 or aex-2 decreased locomotor activity and reversal frequency early during 48 hours of anoxia, suggesting that nlp-40 and aex-2 are required for the proper execution of these behaviors. We found that neuronal knockdown of nlp-40 recapitulated the behaviors observed in nlp-40 mutant animals and increased survival; however, restoring aex-2 function in glr-1 interneurons or motor neurons was sufficient to rescue behaviors to wild-type and restore vulnerability to anoxia. Conclusions: Overall, our results suggest that NLP-40 and AEX-2 likely function in cholinergic or glr-1 interneurons or motor neurons to regulate escape behaviors during anoxia. Escape behaviors are part of the homeostatic response and are typically protective in the wild; however, in our paradigm, we show that loss of either nlp-40 or aex-2 reduces escape responses and confers protection against 48 hours of anoxia. Collectively, these results highlight a new role for NLP-40 and AEX-2 in anoxia and shed light on mechanisms underlying the adaptive responses to anoxia.

papers.title: Disease-associated variants alter a novel physiological role of hnRNP H2 in neuronal development
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein H2 (hnRNP H2) is a member of the hnRNP family of RNA-binding proteins that regulate neuronal function through multiple aspects of RNA metabolism. Mutations in the nuclear localisation signal (NLS) and quasi-RNA recognition motifs (qRRMs) of hnRNP H2 have recently been linked to a severe developmental syndrome, termed HNRNPH2-related neurodevelopmental disorder. Despite its emerging importance, the physiological roles of hnRNP H2 in neuronal development and synaptic maturation, and how disease-associated variants alter these processes to drive pathology, remain poorly understood. Here, we show that hnRNP H2 is expressed in hippocampal neurons and localises to the synaptic compartment. Knockdown of hnRNP H2 revealed essential roles of the protein in the regulation of neuronal morphology, dendritic spine maturation, synaptic transmission, and cortical neuronal migration in vivo. Disease-associated hnRNP H2 variants altered protein localisation and activity-dependent synaptic recruitment, resulting in defects in neuronal morphology, in vivo cortical neuronal migration and laminar orientation, dendritic spine maturation, and synaptic function. Together, these findings establish hnRNP H2 as a critical regulator of neurodevelopment and identify a molecular basis for HNRNPH2-related neurodevelopmental disorder.

papers.title: Larger Pre-Speech Auditory Modulation Is Associated With Smaller Corrective Responses To Auditory Errors
papers.abstract: PurposeDuring speech planning, the brain predicts the auditory consequences of its movements and modulates the auditory system--a process called pre-speech auditory modulation (PSAM). We investigated the link between PSAM and behavioral error correction and determined how aging influences these mechanisms. MethodsSeventeen young adults (18-32 years) and 13 older adults (50-85 years) performed a speaking task involving auditory feedback perturbations and a silent reading control. We measured electrophysiological responses (N1/P2) to auditory probes during speech planning and correlated these modulations with the magnitude of participants subsequent behavioral corrective responses. ResultsBoth groups showed significant modulation of N1 and P2. However, N1 modulation correlated with corrective responses only in young adults. Older adults showed reduced behavioral corrections and smaller, delayed P2 components. Despite these age-related behavioral differences and the loss of the modulation-correction correlation, older adults maintained modulation magnitudes comparable to those of younger adults. ConclusionsN1 modulation serves as a neural index of the brains predictive processes during speech planning. Aging appears to selectively disrupt the integration of these signals into motor output rather than the internal generation of the predictions themselves.

papers.title: Acceleration of vision changes object representations from infancy to adulthood
papers.abstract: While much of the neural and cognitive machinery for visual perception is in place within weeks from birth, we identified and quantified a fundamental difference between infant and adult vision: the temporal rate at which meaningful visual information can be reliably extracted. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography with rapid serial visual presentation, we found that object categorization at 4 and 9 months is respectively seven times and two to three times slower than in adults. Using quantitative information from infants experiments, we created and presented accelerated visual streams to adults, to match infants perceptual experience. We used deep convolutional neural networks to identify object representations that match those elicited in adults when accelerating the information flow. Results show that acceleration compromises finer-grained object distinction while sparing broad, general object representations. We propose that slow vision is a design feature of early development for preserving and highlighting the most stable and general features of the world.

papers.title: Intracranial electrophysiology reveals distinct neural representations of nociception and salience in the human brain
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging studies have shown close overlap between neural representations of nociceptive stimuli and non-nociceptive, salient stimuli (such as low-probability sounds), leading to the proposal that nociception and salience share a common neural substrate in the human brain. Here we use high-resolution intracranial recordings from 13 neurosurgical patients (2,018 total electrodes) to show that neural representations of nociception and salience are anatomically and functionally distinct in the human brain. 77% of 107 electrodes that encoded nociceptive stimuli did not encode low-probability sounds ("nociceptive representations"), whereas 23% encoded both nociceptive and low-probability sounds ("salience representations"). Nociceptive representations were distinct from salience representations in terms of anatomical prevalence (posterior insula, inferior parietal, and perirolandic cortex vs. anterior insula, thalamus, and inferior frontal gyrus), timing (nociception preceded salience by 120 ms on a trial-by-trial basis), and function (intracranial electrical stimulation was more likely to cause sensory experience when applied near nociceptive representations, as compared to salience representations). These results provide strong evidence that nociception and salience have distinct neural substrates in the human brain, and that selective measurement of these distinct processes may help understand patient-to-patient variability in chronic pain and develop personalized brain stimulation treatments.

papers.title: Voluntary engagement predicts recovery across rehabilitation time points after experimental spinal cord injury
papers.abstract: Rehabilitation is the cornerstone of clinical care following spinal cord injury (SCI) and is frequently incorporated into preclinical studies to evaluate emerging therapies. However, the variables that influence the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions in rodent models remain poorly characterized, limiting the translational value of preclinical research. Here, we performed a meta-analysis of 150 preclinical studies comprising more than 3000 rodents and 292 effect sizes to identify such factors associated with successful rehabilitation after SCI. Rehabilitation improved functional outcomes across multiple behavioral domains, with larger effects observed in thoracic than cervical injury models. Meta-regression identified environmental enrichment as the most effective strategy, particularly when combined with task-specific training. Longer rehabilitation duration was associated with improved recovery, whereas greater daily exposure to forced rehabilitation was associated with smaller gains. In contrast, prolonged access to voluntary rehabilitation did not show this relationship. Rehabilitation improved outcomes when initiated at all time points after injury, with greater benefits when initiated during the late subacute and intermediate phases. Rehabilitation approaches associated with higher stress burden produced reduced benefits, suggesting that stress may limit rehabilitation-induced recovery. Collectively, these findings identify rehabilitation type, duration, and delivery context as important determinants of recovery after SCI and support a broad therapeutic window for intervention. Our results favor low-stress, voluntary rehabilitation strategies that promote sustained engagement and provide principles for designing effective and biologically appropriate rehabilitation strategies, potentially improving translational success for emerging SCI therapies. One Sentence SummarySustained voluntary rehabilitation promotes functional recovery across stages of experimental spinal cord injury, whereas prolonged forced training may reduce its benefits.

papers.title: The Effective Visual Acuity of Butterflies in Flight
papers.abstract: The spatial visual acuity of an eye is determined by both the spatial sampling density of the retina and the angular sensitivity of individual photoreceptors. In insect compound eyes, these are respectively characterised by the interommatidial angle, {Delta}{varphi}, and photoreceptor acceptance angle, {Delta}{rho}. During movement, however, finite photoreceptor integration times cause retinal image motion to broaden the effective acceptance angle, potentially degrading spatial resolution beyond its anatomical limit. This problem is especially acute in flying insects, which experience large rotational velocities during locomotion and must actively stabilise gaze to limit retinal image motion. Butterflies present a particularly demanding case because their flight is characterised by large, wingbeat-coupled thoracic oscillations. Here, we quantify how gaze stabilisation limits motion blur in freely flying Monarch butterflies Danaus plexippus by combining free-flight kinematic reconstruction of the head and thorax with separate intracellular measurements of photoreceptor acceptance angles and integration times from quiescent butterflies. We found that, without head compensation, thoracic oscillations would broaden the effective photoreceptor acceptance angle from its quiescent value of 2.17{degrees} to 9.38{degrees} during take-off. Compensatory head movements substantially reduced this motion-induced broadening, limiting the effective acceptance angle to 5.28{degrees}. Nevertheless, this 2.4-fold broadening of effective photoreceptor acceptance angle represents a substantial degradation of spatial acuity in flight, highlighting motion blur as an important constraint on the visual ecology of flying butterflies.

papers.title: Bone regulates locomotion by sustaining motoneuronal mitochondrial function
papers.abstract: Body-brain communication is crucial for optimal neuronal performance across the lifespan, yet whether peripheral organs regulate spinal cord motoneuron (MN) function through circulating molecules remains unknown. The expression of hormone receptors by spinal MNs raises the possibility that circulating cues allow the spinal cord to sense the body's energetic state and sustain motor activity. Here, we show that the bone-derived hormones osteocalcin (OCN) signals on spinal MNs via its receptor GPR158. GPR158 is selectively enriched in spinal cholinergic MNs, and its loss, globally or specifically in spinal MNs, or the one of OCN, impairs locomotor function and reduces choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) levels. Mechanistically, OCN signaling through GPR158 fine-tunes autophagy, mitophagy and mitochondrial activity in spinal MNs. Restoring any of these processes, by pharmacologically inducing mitophagy or chemogenetically activating mitochondria, is sufficient to rescue the locomotor deficits of Gpr158-deficient mice. Finally, OCN restoration in aged mice reverses age-related locomotor decline through a mechanism that requires MN autophagy and mitophagy. This study reveals that through OCN, the skeleton influences motor functions by fine-tuning motoneuronal mitochondria, and suggests that age-related motor decline is, at least in part, reversible.

papers.title: Cross-Tissue Inflammatory Convergence Supports a Putative Muscle-Brain Axis in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Background Reduced muscle strength is associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that skeletal-muscle aging and AD-related neurodegeneration may share biological mechanisms. Vascular dysfunction, immune activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling have been implicated in both tissues, but the extent of shared cellular and molecular programs remains unclear. We investigated cross-tissue transcriptional programs in aging skeletal muscle and AD-related brain tissue and evaluated whether related signals are detectable in peripheral blood. Methods We analyzed independent, unpaired human transcriptomic datasets from skeletal muscle (23 donors), the SEA-AD middle temporal gyrus atlas (84 donors), and peripheral blood. Donor-aware models identified age-associated changes in muscle and transcriptomic changes across continuous pseudoprogression score (CPS) in brain. Cross-tissue comparisons focused on 30 brain donors within an early CPS window. Shared tissue-derived programs were assessed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and independently tested in frailty bulk-blood and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) whole-blood datasets. CellOracle simulations were used to prioritize candidate transcriptional regulators. Results Aging muscle showed increased inflammatory, extracellular-matrix, and stromal communication programs. During early AD-related brain progression, vascular and immune populations showed increasing inflammatory and matrix-associated activity together with shifts in intercellular communication. Cross-tissue analysis identified six concordantly enriched pathways comprising 109 leading-edge genes in endothelial populations and four pathways comprising 51 genes in myeloid populations. Related peripheral-blood signatures varied across cohorts and cell types. However, in independent frailty and ADNI mild cognitive impairment and AD datasets, 23 of 30 predefined tissue-derived pathway-subset tests showed significant positive enrichment after false-discovery-rate correction, whereas individual gene-level bulk-blood associations did not survive correction. CellOracle analyses prioritized ETS2 and BHLHE40 as exploratory endothelial regulators whose simulated perturbation consistently reduced selected shared program scores across tissues. Conclusions Aging skeletal muscle and AD-related brain tissue exhibit convergent endothelial and myeloid inflammatory programs, with related pathway-level signals detectable in peripheral blood. These cross-tissue programs and candidate endothelial regulators provide testable hypotheses for mechanisms linking systemic aging, muscle dysfunction, and AD-related neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Dorsomedial striatal Bmal1 deletion in medium spiny neurons alters EPSCs and dendritic morphology after chronic exposure to alcohol in female mice.
papers.abstract: Circadian clock genes in the striatum modulate alcohol drinking behavior in female mice, but the underlying synaptic mechanisms remain unknown. Medium spiny neurons (MSNs) of the striatum express D1- or D2-type dopamine receptors, which are differentially modulated by alcohol. Here we used whole-cell patch-clamp recordings to examine how deletion of the clock gene Bmal1 affects spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in electrophysiologically identified D1 and D2 neurons of the female mouse dorsomedial striatum (DMS). Prior intermittent access to alcohol increased sEPSC amplitude in putative D1 neurons of wildtype mice without affecting sEPSC frequency, and this increase was accompanied by greater dendritic branching and complexity in biocytin-filled D1 MSNs. Bmal1 knockout had the opposite effect in D1 neurons, reducing sEPSC amplitude in both alcohol-exposed and alcohol-naive animals. In D2 neurons, alcohol produced only a non-significant trend toward increased sEPSC amplitude in wildtype mice, but a significant increase in Bmal1 knockout mice. Thus, local disruption of Bmal1 appears to block the alcohol-induced enhancement of sEPSCs in D1 neurons while unmasking a similar enhancement in D2 neurons. These findings may help explain how Bmal1 deletion in the DMS reduces alcohol consumption in female mice.

papers.title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
papers.abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

papers.title: Impaired astrocytic Cx43 syncytial network in lateral habenula affects synaptic connectivity and drives adolescent stress-induced depression
papers.abstract: Adolescent depression is a major neuropsychiatric disorder induced by early life stress; the underlying cellular mechanisms instigating pathological circuit malformation remain unclear, and, consequently, effective therapeutic strategy is limited. Here, we analysed the contribution of astrocytes to early life stress-induced adolescent depression using a mouse model of parental separation. We identified a previously unrecognised regional specialisation of lateral habenula (LHb) astrocytes, characterised by compact cellular domains, abundant leaflets, and enhanced Cx43 gap junctional coupling. Parental separation selectively reduced astrocytic Cx43 expression and gap junctional communication in the LHb, which was accompanied by profound astrocytic atrophy and loss of leaflets. Single-cell sequencing further revealed that parental separation induces a broad reorganisation of LHb astrocyte transcriptional states, including metabolic, stress-response, and inflammatory programs; moreover, it specifically reduces astrocyte-neuron communication. Consistent with this, we found that structural remodelling of LHb astrocytes affected tripartite synapse geometry, resulting in impaired excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission, and neuronal Ca2+ hyperexcitability, all ultimately associated with depressive-like behaviours. Selective knockdown of astrocytic Cx43 in the LHb recapitulated these pathological changes and translated into depressive-like behaviours. Mechanistically, we found that impaired Cx43 gap junctional communication is associated with excessive astrocytic Ca2+ dynamics, resulting in Rac1-GTPase activation and decreased p-Ezrin levels. In vivo inhibition of LHb astrocytic Ca2+ signalling rescued astrocytic atrophy and depressive-like behaviours following parental separation. Together, our findings establish a Cx43-Ca2+-Rac1-p-Ezrin pathway that links gap junction malfunction to structural remodelling of astrocytes and disruption of neuron-astrocyte interactions in the developing LHb. Our study reveals astrocytic Ca2+ dysregulation as an active downstream effector of Cx43 dysfunction and identifies a regionally specialised astrocytic mechanism through which early-life stress disrupts synaptic transmission and neuronal function during adolescence, providing a potential cellular target for intervention in adolescent depression.

papers.title: Focal drug uncaging for the precise control of endogenous nicotinic receptors in behaving mice
papers.abstract: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors shape diverse brain functions, including reward, aversion, and pain, but dissecting their roles in vivo requires drug delivery with spatiotemporal precision that conventional pharmacology cannot provide. Here we establish in vivo photopharmacology of endogenous nicotinic receptors: two complementary, highly-potent agonists, administered systemically in an inactive caged form, are photoreleased locally in target brain circuits of behaving wild-type mice. Despite irreversible photochemistry, photoactivation can be repeated over many trials on a minute timescale, for hours following a single injection. Local uncaging evokes circuit-specific dopamine release, drives place preference from the ventral tegmental area and aversion from the interpeduncular nucleus, and, in pain circuits, reveals a pronociceptive effect masked when the same agonists are given systemically. By controlling where and when nicotinic signaling acts, this approach exposes circuit-specific drug effects invisible to conventional pharmacology, and outlines a general strategy for on-demand control of endogenous receptors in vivo.
